name: Brush cut

lead: A brush cut keeps the top of the hair short in every dimension, around 6 to 13 mm, following the shape of the head, with the lower sides and back tapered with clippers. It is closely related to the crew cut and flat top.
It matters for looks because very short hair shows off the head and jawline and needs little styling, and an upright front can add a bit of lift at the forehead.

paras: It is cut by a barber with clippers and shears, often with the front slightly longer, and traditionally styled with a firm wax. Thick hair that stands up suits it best, and barbers tailor the shape to face and skull shape.
No medical risks. It leaves little hair to hide hairline or scalp features, and thin or very soft hair may not stand up.

angle.text: A brush cut replaces hair length with a clean, structured outline, so the head shape and jaw read more clearly. A slightly longer front can add a little height at the hairline.

lead: The brush cut is a short haircut in which the top is cut to a uniform short length, about 6 to 13 mm, following the head's contour, while the lower sides and back are tapered with clippers as in a crew cut [1]. Cuts shorter than a quarter inch are called burrs [1].

The style is historically associated with the military and was later adopted by subcultures such as punk [1]. Wikipedia's crew-cut article notes that the 'brush cut' name existed in English since at least the mid-1700s, that college rowing teams helped popularise the short cut, and that it was widespread among US college students in the 1920s and 1930s and among GI-era veterans afterwards [2].
It is generally styled with a firm 'brush wax', and the final shape can be tailored to face shape, skull shape and hairline [1][2].
infobox: Crew cut, flat top, burr, buzz cut

paras: The top and upper back and sides are the same length and follow the head, with variants that grade the top slightly longer toward the front or graduate the front hairline for lift [1]. The crew cut, flat top, butch and Ivy League cuts are all regarded as types of buzz cut; the flat top flattens the top into a level plane [2].

Military adoption and later punk use are noted in Wikipedia's article [1]. The crew-cut article describes college and WWII-era popularity, a decline when long hair was fashionable from the mid-1960s and a return in the late 1970s and early 1980s, with the flat top the most popular version in the 1980s [2].
Cutting uses clippers and shears over a comb or freehand, and thick hair that stands up easily is described as best suited [1][2].
